candidates.speaker: Joe Folley
candidates.proposition: A libertarian appeal to live options needs a principled account of when an alternative is genuinely available, especially because people continue to blame agents whose upbringing appears to exclude such alternatives.
candidates.attributionBasis: The turn follows Nathan Hawkins's account of constrained live options and is framed in the first person as an incompatibilist challenge before discussing Jojo evidence.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The challenge directly tests whether alternative possibilities can explain responsibility judgments without an independent and workable criterion for identifying which possibilities were live.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Nathan Hawkins's claim that agents lacking any genuinely live alternative are not morally responsible.

candidates.contextSummary: After Hawkins treats biological and social constraints as compatible with freedom inside a remaining range of live options, Folley presses the epistemic boundary of that range and invokes responsibility judgments about Jojo.

candidates.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
candidates.proposition: Libertarian responsibility rests not merely on isolated present choices but on an agent's alternative-capable role in gradually shaping the character from which later settled conduct proceeds.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly identifies his position as libertarian, answers the Jojo example, and develops a first-person account of character formation and responsibility.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move supplies both libertarian requirements named by the motion—doing otherwise and sourcehood—while explaining moral responsibility through cumulative self-formation under constraints.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Joe Folley's challenge that live-option restrictions resemble deterministic prediction and fail to match continuing blame of Jojo.

candidates.contextSummary: Hawkins answers the Jojo objection by arguing that respondents struggle to imagine a person wholly without resistance, then shifts from proximal choices to the accumulated decisions that form character.

candidates.speaker: Joe Folley
candidates.proposition: Determinism can preserve will and responsibility through closed causal loops, proximal causation, and character models that predict an agent's conduct, without requiring genuine alternatives.
candidates.attributionBasis: The turn directly questions why Hawkins's character-formation story is incompatible with determinism and consistently develops the deterministic alternative in Folley's voice.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is a direct compatibilist account of agency and responsibility under determinism, offering proximal sourcehood and causally effective character in place of libertarian alternatives.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Nathan Hawkins's contention that responsibility for character depends on alternative-capable choices made throughout a person's development.

candidates.contextSummary: Following Hawkins's cumulative self-formation account, Folley argues that upbringing can initiate a determined path while the resulting person still functions as a causal agent whose character explains later behavior.

candidates.speaker: Joe Folley
candidates.proposition: Freedom and responsibility are plural, practice-shaped concepts whose useful content should be reconstructed from praise, blame, and reactive attitudes rather than forced into one metaphysically necessary-and-sufficient formula.
candidates.attributionBasis: Folley continues the same uninterrupted turn, surveys several compatibilist traditions, and explicitly advances a pragmatic reconstruction from responsibility practices.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move reframes the debate's governing standard: compatibilism need not reproduce one libertarian essence if multiple agency concepts successfully organize responsibility and social practice.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The libertarian framing that a single metaphysical condition of alternative possibility grounds and explains moral responsibility.

candidates.contextSummary: Folley notes that blame survives deterministic framing and that coercion can undermine freedom even with alternatives, then treats freedom, choice, and responsibility as related but nonidentical practical concepts.

candidates.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
candidates.proposition: If pragmatism takes deliberative phenomenology and practical causal reasoning seriously, it should regard agents as ultimate sources and their apparent ability to do otherwise as true rather than metaphysically irrelevant.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker announces an attempt to persuade Joe toward libertarianism on Joe's pragmatic grounds and develops the argument using deliberation, causation, and responsibility.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The argument seeks to derive both sourcehood and alternative possibilities from the compatibilist's own pragmatic starting point, directly supporting the libertarian side of the motion.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Joe Folley's pragmatic proposal to begin with the practical work of freedom and responsibility ascriptions rather than libertarian metaphysics.

candidates.contextSummary: Hawkins accepts the turn toward lived practices but argues that causal reasoning presents the deliberator as the originating cause, while responsibility practices treat unchosen alternatives as genuinely available.

candidates.speaker: Joe Folley
candidates.proposition: The ineliminable first-person experience of deliberating as though one could do otherwise creates a serious unresolved challenge for a deterministic compatibilism that remains available from third-person perspectives.
candidates.attributionBasis: Folley explicitly labels the issue a worry for his own view, contrasts his attitude toward other agents with his self-conception, and acknowledges lacking a settled solution.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This concession identifies a major internal pressure on compatibilism: deterministic theory may be sustainable for others while failing to govern the agent's own unavoidable deliberative standpoint.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Nathan Hawkins's argument that pragmatic attention to deliberation commits agents to subjective sourcehood and genuine alternatives.

candidates.contextSummary: Folley distinguishes a thicker pragmatist notion of truth from mere usefulness but accepts that he may be unable to understand his own deliberation without treating himself as able to do otherwise.

candidates.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
candidates.proposition: Because evolved conscious deliberation and inquiry are practically indispensable, pragmatism should validate their alternative-possibility structure, and interpersonal interpretation likewise resists denying agency to everyone except oneself.
candidates.attributionBasis: Hawkins introduces two explicit further challenges, addresses Joe by name, and links evolutionary usefulness, inquiry, and interpersonal reactive attitudes to libertarian agency.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move strengthens the pragmatic case for alternatives and attacks the proposed first-person exception by arguing that ordinary interpretation also distinguishes genuine agency in other people.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Joe Folley's tentative position that first-person deliberation may require alternatives even though other agents can still be understood compatibilistically.

candidates.contextSummary: After Folley concedes a first-person difficulty, Hawkins argues first that evolution and inquiry vindicate deliberative alternatives and second that Folley's treatment of others already tracks agent-versus-excuse distinctions.

candidates.speaker: Joe Folley
candidates.proposition: A proximal-source distinction between choices and nonchoices can survive proven determinism, while the conflict between objective study and first-person deliberation is a near-universal problem rather than a special failure of compatibilism.
candidates.attributionBasis: Following Hawkins's request for the useful notion, Folley repeatedly identifies proximal sourcehood as his view and develops the object-versus-subject naturalism problem.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move offers a positive compatibilist basis for agency without alternatives and limits the force of the first-person objection by generalizing it across theories of human inquiry.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Nathan Hawkins's demand for a useful nonlibertarian source notion and his argument that deliberative agency extends to interpretations of other people.

candidates.contextSummary: Folley says deterministic truth would not erase the distinction between choices and nonchoices, then explains how inquiry becomes reflexively difficult once human deliberators are also treated as empirical objects.

candidates.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
candidates.proposition: Blurring the objective-subjective divide supports an idealist picture in which subjectivity belongs within the world itself, making nature's indeterminacy and selection more intelligible as mind-like rather than merely mechanical.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker responds affirmatively to Folley's subject-object problem, contrasts idealism with reductive objectivism, and presents the mind-like-world proposal as a possible solution.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The proposal supplies a broader metaphysical setting in which libertarian subjectivity and natural indeterminacy can coexist, supporting sourcehood even though it is less direct than earlier arguments.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Joe Folley's claim that reconciling the human being as both inquirer and object of inquiry is a near-universal unresolved problem.

candidates.contextSummary: Hawkins treats pragmatism and idealism as responses to the collapse of a strict subject-object division, then suggests that patterns of randomness and selection indicate a more subject-like world.
